items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. In our power are opinion (ὑπόληψις), movement towards a thing (ὁρμή), desire, aversion (ἔκκλισις, turning from a thing); and in a word, whatever are our own acts: not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices (magisterial power), and in a word, whatever are not our own acts. And the things in our power are by nature free, not subject to restraint nor hindrance: but the things not in our power are weak, slavish, subject to restraint, in the power of others. Remember then that if you think the things which are by nature slavish to be free, and the things which are in the power of others to be your own, you will be hindered, you will lament, you will be disturbed, you will blame both gods and men: but if you think that only which is your own to be your own, and if you think that what is another’s, as it really is, belongs to another, no man will ever compel you, no man will hinder you, you will never blame any man, you will accuse no man, you will do nothing involuntarily (against your will), no man will harm you, you will have no enemy, for you will not suffer any harm…

In our power are opinion, movement towards a thing, desire, aversion; and in a word, whatever are our own acts: not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices, and in a word, whatever are not our own acts. And the things in our power are by nature free, not subject to restraint nor hindrance: but the things not in our power are weak, slavish, subject to restraint, in the power of others. Remember then that if you think the things which are by nature slavish to be free, and the things which are in the power of others to be your own, you will be hindered, you will lament, you will be disturbed, you will blame both gods and men: but if you think that only which is your own to be your own, and if you think that what is another’s, as it really is, belongs to another, no man will ever compel you, no man will hinder you, you will never blame any man, you will accuse no man, you will do nothing involuntarily, no man will harm you, you will have no enemy, for you will not suffer any harm…

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Straightway then practise saying to every harsh appearance, You are an appearance, and in no manner what you appear to be.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things: for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were, it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death, that it is terrible, is the terrible thing. When then we are impeded or disturbed or grieved, let us never blame others, but ourselves, that is, our opinions. It is the act of an ill-instructed man to blame others for his own bad condition; it is the act of one who has begun to be instructed, to lay the blame on himself; and of one whose instruction is completed, neither to blame another, nor himself.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things…

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: It is the act of an ill-instructed man to blame others for his own bad condition; it is the act of one who has begun to be instructed, to lay the blame on himself; and of one whose instruction is completed, neither to blame another, nor himself.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: On the occasion of every accident (event) that befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and inquire what power you have for turning it to use. If you see a fair man or a fair woman, you will find that the power to resist is temperance (continence). If labour (pain) be presented to you, you will find that it is endurance. If it be abusive words, you will find it to be patience. And if you have been thus formed to the (proper) habit, the appearances will not carry you along with them.
items.display_text: On the occasion of every accident that befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and inquire what power you have for turning it to use. If you see a fair man or a fair woman, you will find that the power to resist is temperance. If labour be presented to you, you will find that it is endurance. If it be abusive words, you will find it to be patience. And if you have been thus formed to the habit, the appearances will not carry you along with them.
items.display_edit: translator's parenthetical glosses removed for on-screen text; 'text' remains verbatim

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Begin then from little things. Is the oil spilled? Is a little wine stolen? Say on the occasion, at such price is sold freedom from perturbation; at such price is sold tranquillity, but nothing is got for nothing.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: If you would improve, submit to be considered without sense and foolish with respect to externals.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: He is the master of every man who has the power over the things, which another person wishes or does not wish, the power to confer them on him or to take them away. Whoever then wishes to be free, let him neither wish for anything nor avoid anything which depends on others: if he does not observe this rule, he must be a slave.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Remember that in life you ought to behave as at a banquet. Suppose that something is carried round and is opposite to you. Stretch out your hand and take a portion with decency. Suppose that it passes by you. Do not detain it. Suppose that it is not yet come to you. Do not send your desire forward to it, but wait till it is opposite to you. Do so with respect to children, so with respect to a wife, so with respect to magisterial offices, so with respect to wealth, and you will be some time a worthy partner of the banquets of the gods…

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Remember that thou art an actor in a play, of such a kind as the teacher (author) may choose; if short, of a short one; if long, of a long one: if he wishes you to act the part of a poor man, see that you act the part naturally; if the part of a lame man, of a magistrate, of a private person, (do the same). For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.

For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: You can be invincible, if you enter into no contest in which it is not in your power to conquer.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting. When then a man irritates you, you must know that it is your own opinion which has irritated you. Therefore especially try not to be carried away by the appearance. For if you once gain time and delay, you will more easily master yourself.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: When then a man irritates you, you must know that it is your own opinion which has irritated you.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Let death and exile and every other thing which appears dreadful be daily before your eyes; but most of all death: and you will never think of anything mean nor will you desire anything extravagantly.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: If you desire philosophy, prepare yourself from the beginning to be ridiculed, to expect that many will sneer at you, and say, He has all at once returned to us as a philosopher; and whence does he get this supercilious look for us? Do you not show a supercilious look; but hold on to the things which seem to you best as one appointed by God to this station. And remember that if you abide in the same principles, these men who first ridiculed will afterwards admire you: but if you shall have been overpowered by them, you will bring on yourself double ridicule.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: If it should ever happen to you to be turned to externals in order to please some person, you must know that you have lost your purpose in life.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: If any person was intending to put your body in the power of any man whom you fell in with on the way, you would be vexed: but that you put your understanding in the power of any man whom you meet, so that if he should revile you, it is disturbed and troubled, are you not ashamed at this?

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: A man wishes to conquer at the Olympic games. I also wish indeed, for it is a fine thing. But observe both the things which come first, and the things which follow; and then begin the act. You must do everything according to rule, eat according to strict orders, abstain from delicacies, exercise yourself as you are bid at appointed times, in heat, in cold, you must not drink cold water, nor wine as you choose; in a word, you must deliver yourself up to the exercise master as you do to the physician, and then proceed to the contest. And sometimes you will strain the hand, put the ankle out of joint, swallow much dust, sometimes be flogged, and after all this be defeated. When you have considered all this, if you still choose, go to the contest…

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: If a man has reported to you, that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make any defence (answer) to what has been told you: but reply, The man did not know the rest of my faults, for he would not have mentioned these only.
items.display_text: If a man has reported to you, that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make any defence to what has been told you: but reply, The man did not know the rest of my faults, for he would not have mentioned these only.
items.display_edit: translator's parenthetical glosses removed for on-screen text; 'text' remains verbatim

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Immediately prescribe some character and some form to yourself, which you shall observe both when you are alone and when you meet with men.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: In company take care not to speak much and excessively about your own acts or dangers: for as it is pleasant to you to make mention of your own dangers, it is not so pleasant to others to hear what has happened to you.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: If you have received the impression (φαντασίαν) of any pleasure, guard yourself against being carried away by it; but let the thing wait for you, and allow yourself a certain delay on your own part. Then think of both times, of the time when you will enjoy the pleasure, and of the time after the enjoyment of the pleasure when you will repent and will reproach yourself. And set against these things how you will rejoice if you have abstained from the pleasure, and how you will commend yourself. But if it seem to you seasonable to undertake (do) the thing, take care that the charm of it, and the pleasure, and the attraction of it shall not conquer you: but set on the other side the consideration how much better it is to be conscious that you have gained this victory.
items.display_text: If you have received the impression of any pleasure, guard yourself against being carried away by it; but let the thing wait for you, and allow yourself a certain delay on your own part. Then think of both times, of the time when you will enjoy the pleasure, and of the time after the enjoyment of the pleasure when you will repent and will reproach yourself. And set against these things how you will rejoice if you have abstained from the pleasure, and how you will commend yourself. But if it seem to you seasonable to undertake the thing, take care that the charm of it, and the pleasure, and the attraction of it shall not conquer you: but set on the other side the consideration how much better it is to be conscious that you have gained this victory.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: When you have decided that a thing ought to be done and are doing it, never avoid being seen doing it, though the many shall form an unfavourable opinion about it. For if it is not right to do it, avoid doing the thing; but if it is right, why are you afraid of those who shall find fault wrongly?

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: In walking about as you take care not to step on a nail or to sprain your foot, so take care not to damage your own ruling faculty: and if we observe this rule in every act, we shall undertake the act with more security.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: When any person treats you ill or speaks ill of you, remember that he does this or says this because he thinks that it is his duty. It is not possible then for him to follow that which seems right to you, but that which seems right to himself. Accordingly if he is wrong in his opinion, he is the person who is hurt, for he is the person who has been deceived; for if a man shall suppose the true conjunction to be false, it is not the conjunction which is hindered, but the man who has been deceived about it. If you proceed then from these opinions, you will be mild in temper to him who reviles you: for say on each occasion, It seemed so to him.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold of the act by that handle wherein he acts unjustly, for this is the handle which cannot be borne: but lay hold of the other, that he is your brother, that he was nurtured with you, and you will lay hold of the thing by that handle by which it can be borne.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: These reasonings do not cohere: I am richer than you, therefore I am better than you; I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am better than you. On the contrary these rather cohere, I am richer than you, therefore my possessions are greater than yours: I am more eloquent than you, therefore my speech is superior to yours. But you are neither possession nor speech.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: On no occasion call yourself a philosopher, and do not speak much among the uninstructed about theorems (philosophical rules, precepts): but do that which follows from them. For example at a banquet do not say how a man ought to eat, but eat as you ought to eat.
items.display_text: On no occasion call yourself a philosopher, and do not speak much among the uninstructed about theorems: but do that which follows from them. For example at a banquet do not say how a man ought to eat, but eat as you ought to eat.
items.display_edit: translator's parenthetical glosses removed for on-screen text; 'text' remains verbatim

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: For even sheep do not vomit up their grass and show to the shepherds how much they have eaten; but when they have internally digested the pasture, they produce externally wool and milk. Do you also show not your theorems to the uninstructed, but show the acts which come from their digestion.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: And when a man shall say to you, that you know nothing, and you are not vexed, then be sure that you have begun the work (of philosophy).
items.display_text: And when a man shall say to you, that you know nothing, and you are not vexed, then be sure that you have begun the work.
items.display_edit: translator's parenthetical glosses removed for on-screen text; 'text' remains verbatim

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: And if you ever wish to exercise yourself in labour and endurance, do it for yourself, and not for others…

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: The condition and characteristic of an uninstructed person is this: he never expects from himself profit (advantage) nor harm, but from externals. The condition and characteristic of a philosopher is this: he expects all advantage and all harm from himself. The signs (marks) of one who is making progress are these: he censures no man, he praises no man, he blames no man, he accuses no man, he says nothing about himself as if he were somebody or knew something; when he is impeded at all or hindered, he blames himself: if a man praises him, he ridicules the praiser to himself: if a man censures him, he makes no defence…
items.display_text: The condition and characteristic of an uninstructed person is this: he never expects from himself profit nor harm, but from externals. The condition and characteristic of a philosopher is this: he expects all advantage and all harm from himself. The signs of one who is making progress are these: he censures no man, he praises no man, he blames no man, he accuses no man, he says nothing about himself as if he were somebody or knew something; when he is impeded at all or hindered, he blames himself: if a man praises him, he ridicules the praiser to himself: if a man censures him, he makes no defence…

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: And whatever any man shall say about you, do not attend to it: for this is no affair of yours.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: How long will you then still defer thinking yourself worthy of the best things, and in no matter transgressing the distinctive reason? Have you accepted the theorems (rules), which it was your duty to agree to, and have you agreed to them? what teacher then do you still expect that you defer to him the correction of yourself? You are no longer a youth, but already a full-grown man. If then you are negligent and slothful, and are continually making procrastination after procrastination, and proposal (intention) after proposal, and fixing day after day, after which you will attend to yourself, you will not know that you are not making improvement, but you will continue ignorant (uninstructed) both while you live and till you die. Immediately then think it right to live as a full-grown man, and one who is making proficiency, and let everything which appears to you to be the best be to you a law which must not be transgressed. And if anything laborious, or pleasant or glorious or inglorious be presented to you, remember that now is the contest, now are the Olympic games, and they cannot be deferred; and that it depends on one defeat and one giving way that progress is either lost or maintained. Socrates in this way became perfect, in all things improving himself, attending to nothing except to reason. But you, though you are not yet a Socrates, ought to live as one who wishes to be a Socrates.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (via Arrian)
items.text: Therefore we lie; but the demonstration that we ought not to lie we have ready to hand.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: If you wish to be good, first believe that you are bad.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: It is better to do wrong seldom and to own it, and to act right for the most part, than seldom to admit that you have done wrong and to do wrong often.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Check (punish) your passions (πάφη), that you may not be punished by them.
items.display_text: Check your passions, that you may not be punished by them.
items.display_edit: translator's parenthetical glosses removed for on-screen text; 'text' remains verbatim

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: No man who loves money, and loves pleasure, and loves fame, also loves mankind, but only he who loves virtue.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: As you would not choose to sail in a large and decorated and gold-laden ship (or ship ornamented with gold), and to be drowned; so do not choose to dwell in a large and costly house and to be disturbed (by cares).
items.display_text: As you would not choose to sail in a large and decorated and gold-laden ship, and to be drowned; so do not choose to dwell in a large and costly house and to be disturbed.
items.display_edit: translator's parenthetical glosses removed for on-screen text; 'text' remains verbatim

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Examine yourself whether you wish to be rich or to be happy. If you wish to be rich, you should know that it is neither a good thing nor at all in your power: but if you wish to be happy, you should know that it is both a good thing and in your power, for the one is a temporary loan of fortune, and happiness comes from the will.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: It is not poverty which produces sorrow, but desire; nor does wealth release from fear, but reason (the power of reasoning, λογισμός). If then you acquire this power of reasoning, you will neither desire wealth nor complain of poverty.
items.display_text: It is not poverty which produces sorrow, but desire; nor does wealth release from fear, but reason. If then you acquire this power of reasoning, you will neither desire wealth nor complain of poverty.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Instead of an herd of oxen, endeavour to assemble herds of friends in your house.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Nothing is smaller (meaner) than love of pleasure, and love of gain and pride. Nothing is superior to magnanimity, and gentleness, and love of mankind, and beneficence.
items.display_text: Nothing is smaller than love of pleasure, and love of gain and pride. Nothing is superior to magnanimity, and gentleness, and love of mankind, and beneficence.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: As a goose is not frightened by cackling nor a sheep by bleating, so let not the clamour of a senseless multitude alarm you.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: As the sun does not wait for prayers and incantations to be induced to rise, but immediately shines and is saluted by all: so do you also not wait for clappings of hands, and shouts and praise to be induced to do good, but be a doer of good voluntarily, and you will be beloved as much as the sun.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Neither should a ship rely on one small anchor, nor should life rest on a single hope.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: What we ought not to do, we should not even think of doing.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Deliberate much before saying or doing anything, for you will not have the power of recalling what has been said or done.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: To admonish is better than to reproach: for admonition is mild and friendly, but reproach is harsh and insulting; and admonition corrects those who are doing wrong, but reproach only convicts them.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: No man is free who is not master of himself.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: In prosperity it is very easy to find a friend; but in adversity it is most difficult of all things.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: He is a wise man who does not grieve for the things which he has not, but rejoices for those which he has.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Epictetus being asked how a man should give pain to his enemy answered, By preparing himself to live the best life that he can.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Fortify yourself with contentment, for this is an impregnable fortress.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Nature has given to men one tongue, but two ears, that we may hear from others twice as much as we speak.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Choose the best life, for custom (habit) will make it pleasant.
items.display_text: Choose the best life, for custom will make it pleasant.
items.display_edit: translator's parenthetical glosses removed for on-screen text; 'text' remains verbatim

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: The necessity of circumstances proves friends and detects enemies.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: When our friends are present, we ought to treat them well; and when they are absent, to speak of them well.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Let no man think that he is loved by any man when he loves no man.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: If you wish to live a life free from sorrow, think of what is going to happen as if it had already happened.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Those who have been instructed, like those who have been trained in the palaestra, though they may have fallen, rise again from their misfortune quickly and skilfully.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: When a young man was boasting in the theatre and saying, I am wise, for I have conversed with many wise men; Epictetus said, I also have conversed with many rich men, but I am not rich.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Epictetus being asked, What man is rich, answered, He who is content (who has enough).
items.display_text: Epictetus being asked, What man is rich, answered, He who is content.
items.display_edit: translator's parenthetical glosses removed for on-screen text; 'text' remains verbatim

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Who among us does not admire the act of Lycurgus the Lacedaemonian? For after he was maimed in one of his eyes by one of the citizens, and the young man was delivered up to him by the people that he might punish him as he chose, Lycurgus spared him: and after instructing him and making him a good man he brought him into the theatre. When the Lacedaemonians expressed their surprise, Lycurgus said, I received from you this youth when he was insolent and violent: I restore him to you gentle and a good citizen.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: Pittacus after being wronged by a certain person and having the power of punishing him let him go, saying, Forgiveness is better than revenge: for forgiveness is the sign of a gentle nature, but revenge the sign of a savage nature.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: A pirate had been cast on the land and was perishing through the tempest. A man took clothing and gave it to him, and brought the pirate into his house, and supplied him with everything else that was necessary. When the man was reproached by a person for doing kindness to the bad, he replied, I have shown this regard not to the man, but to mankind.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: attributed to Epictetus in ancient anthologies (Stobaeus, Antonius, Maximus); Long notes some fragments may not be genuine — display as 'attrib.'
items.text: When Archelaus was sending for Socrates to make him rich, Socrates told the messengers to return this answer: At Athens four measures (choenices) of meal are sold for one obolus (the sixth of a drachme), and the fountains run with water: if what I have is not enough (sufficient) for me, yet I am sufficient for what I have, and so it becomes sufficient for me.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: I must die. Must I then die lamenting? I must be put in chains. Must I then also lament? I must go into exile. Does any man then hinder me from going with smiles and cheerfulness and contentment? Tell me the secret which you possess. I will not, for this is in my power. But I will put you in chains. Man, what are you talking about? Me, in chains? You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower. I will throw you into prison. My poor body, you mean. I will cut your head off. When then have I told you that my head alone cannot be cut off? These are the things which philosophers should meditate on, which they should write daily, in which they should exercise themselves.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: What then did Agrippinus say? He said, “I am not a hindrance to myself.” When it was reported to him that his trial was going on in the Senate, he said: “I hope it may turn out well; but it is the fifth hour of the day”—this was the time when he was used to exercise himself and then take the cold bath,—“let us go and take our exercise.” After he had taken his exercise, one comes and tells him, “You have been condemned.” “To banishment,” he replies, “or to death?” “To banishment.” “What about my property?” “It is not taken from you.” “Let us go to Aricia then,” he said, “and dine.”

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Only consider at what price you sell your own will: if for no other reason, at least for this, that you sell it not for a small sum.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Epictetus is not superior to Socrates; but if he is not inferior, this is enough for me; for I shall never be a Milo, and yet I do not neglect my body; nor shall I be a Croesus, and yet I do not neglect my property; nor, in a word, do we neglect looking after anything because we despair of reaching the highest degree.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: What is the product of virtue? Tranquillity.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: …where a man is against his will, there he is in prison. So Socrates was not in prison, for he was there willingly.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: But you ought when you are alone to call this condition by the name of tranquillity and freedom, and to think yourself like to the gods; and when you are with many, you ought not to call it crowd, nor trouble, nor uneasiness, but festival and assembly, and so accept all contentedly.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Nothing great, said Epictetus, is produced suddenly, since not even the grape or the fig is. If you say to me now that you want a fig, I will answer to you that it requires time: let it flower first, then put forth fruit, and then ripen. Is then the fruit of a fig-tree not perfected suddenly and in one hour, and would you possess the fruit of a man’s mind in so short a time and so easily? Do not expect it, even if I tell you.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Nothing great, said Epictetus, is produced suddenly, since not even the grape or the fig is.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Do not admire your clothes, and then you will not be angry with the thief.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: I also lately had an iron lamp placed by the side of my household gods; hearing a noise at the door, I ran down, and found that the lamp had been carried off. I reflected that he who had taken the lamp had done nothing strange. What then? To-morrow, I said, you will find an earthen lamp; for a man only loses that which he has.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: It is not possible that what is by nature free can be disturbed by anything else, or hindered by any other thing than by itself. But it is a man’s own opinions which disturb him.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Who are they by whom you wish to be admired? Are they not those of whom you are used to say that they are mad? Well, then, do you wish to be admired by madmen?

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: It is circumstances (difficulties) which show what men are.
items.display_text: It is circumstances which show what men are.
items.display_edit: translator's parenthetical glosses removed for on-screen text; 'text' remains verbatim

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: It is circumstances (difficulties) which show what men are. Therefore when a difficulty falls upon you, remember that God, like a trainer of wrestlers, has matched you with a rough young man. For what purpose? you may say. Why, that you may become an Olympic conqueror; but it is not accomplished without sweat. In my opinion no man has had a more profitable difficulty than you have had, if you choose to make use of it as an athlete would deal with a young antagonist.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Diogenes, who was sent as a scout before you, made a different report to us. He says that death is no evil, for neither is it base; he says that fame (reputation) is the noise of madmen. And what has this spy said about pain, about pleasure, and about poverty? He says that to be naked is better than any purple robe, and to sleep on the bare ground is the softest bed; and he gives as a proof of each thing that he affirms his own courage, his tranquillity, his freedom, and the healthy appearance and compactness of his body. There is no enemy near, he says; all is peace. How so, Diogenes? “See,” he replies, “if I am struck, if I have been wounded, if I have fled from any man.” This is what a scout ought to be.

He says that to be naked is better than any purple robe, and to sleep on the bare ground is the softest bed; and he gives as a proof of each thing that he affirms his own courage, his tranquillity, his freedom, and the healthy appearance and compactness of his body. There is no enemy near, he says; all is peace. How so, Diogenes? “See,” he replies, “if I am struck, if I have been wounded, if I have fled from any man.” This is what a scout ought to be.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: …remember this general truth, that it is we who squeeze ourselves, who put ourselves in straits; that is, our opinions squeeze us and put us in straits.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: For what is it to be reviled? Stand by a stone and revile it, and what will you gain? If then a man listens like a stone, what profit is there to the reviler?

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: God has fixed this law, and says, “If you would have anything good, receive it from yourself.”

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: And what does Socrates say? “Anytus and Melitus can kill me, but they cannot hurt me.”

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: For it is not these small arguments that are wanted now; the writings of the Stoics are full of them. What then is the thing which is wanted? A man who shall apply them, one who by his acts shall bear testimony to his words.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: …for death or pain is not formidable, but the fear of pain or death.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: What is death? A tragic mask. Turn it and examine it. See, it does not bite.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: …we should rather believe the philosophers who say that the educated only are free.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Therefore Socrates said to one who was reminding him to prepare for his trial, Do you not think then that I have been preparing for it all my life? By what kind of preparation? I have maintained that which was in my own power. How then? I have never done anything unjust either in my private or in my public life.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Things themselves (materials) are indifferent; but the use of them is not indifferent.
items.display_text: Things themselves are indifferent; but the use of them is not indifferent.
items.display_edit: translator's parenthetical glosses removed for on-screen text; 'text' remains verbatim

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: But we should act as we do in the case of a voyage. What can I do? I can choose the master of the ship, the sailors, the day, the opportunity. Then comes a storm. What more have I to care for? for my part is done. The business belongs to another, the master. But the ship is sinking—what then have I to do? I do the only thing that I can, not to be drowned full of fear, nor screaming nor blaming God, but knowing that what has been produced must also perish: for I am not an immortal being, but a man, a part of the whole, as an hour is a part of the day: I must be present like the hour, and past like the hour.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Always remember what is your own, and what belongs to another; and you will not be disturbed.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: For this reason philosophers admonish us not to be satisfied with learning only, but also to add study, and then practice.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: For it is one thing to lay up bread and wine as in a storehouse, and another thing to eat.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: Now this was the first and chief peculiarity of Socrates, never to be irritated in argument, never to utter anything abusive, anything insulting, but to bear with abusive persons and to put an end to the quarrel.

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: When I see a man anxious, I say, What does this man want? If he did not want something which is not in his power, how could he be anxious?

items.author: Epictetus
items.attribution: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian); text from Long's abridged 'Selection from the Discourses' — refs are chapter-level
items.text: For this reason, when Zeno was going to meet Antigonus, he was not anxious, for Antigonus had no power over any of the things which Zeno admired; and Zeno did not care for those things over which Antigonus had power. But Antigonus was anxious when he was going to meet Zeno, for he wished to please Zeno; but this was a thing external (out of his power). But Zeno did not want to please Antigonus; for no man who is skilled in any art wishes to please one who has no such skill.
items.display_text: For this reason, when Zeno was going to meet Antigonus, he was not anxious, for Antigonus had no power over any of the things which Zeno admired; and Zeno did not care for those things over which Antigonus had power. But Antigonus was anxious when he was going to meet Zeno, for he wished to please Zeno; but this was a thing external. But Zeno did not want to please Antigonus; for no man who is skilled in any art wishes to please one who has no such skill.
